chapter_theme: The kaathai of seeing the country: driven by their past deed, Kovalan and Kannaki slip out of Puhar before dawn past its temples and viharas, take the Jain nun Kavunthi as guide, and walk slowly through the Chola country of the Kaveri; a Charana tells Kavunthi that a strong deed returns like a sown seed and cannot be put off, she vows every sense to the Arhat, and at Uraiyur's edge she curses two mockers into jackals and, at the wronged couple's plea, sets them a term of release.

cast.role: Kannaki's husband, a merchant's son of Puhar, setting out for Madurai to recover his wealth
a Jain nun living by the Kaveri outside Puhar, who goes with the couple to Madurai
a Jain Charana, a sky-walking sage, who appears on the stone seat and preaches (named in the honorific plural)
a wanton courtesan who mocks the travellers and is cursed into a jackal
the idle-tongued man with the courtesan, cursed into a jackal with her

silappathikaram:10:1-14.reading: Before dawn on the last dark night of the month, with the deed of the past driving them and their own minds pressing, the couple leave by the long gate of their mansion, pass the temple of the sapphire-hued god asleep on the serpent, and go past the seven Indra viharas where sky-walkers proclaim the word of the dharma-teacher under the five-branched bodhi.
silappathikaram:10:1-14.nuance: Line 4 gives two drivers side by side: ஊழ்வினை pushes and the heart urges (உள்ளம் துரப்ப), so the narrator names the past deed as cause at the very moment the couple act of their own will; Kovalan's own spoken reason, the wish for wealth in Madurai, comes at line 51. The road out of Puhar is a tour of the city's faiths, a Vishnu temple and Buddhist viharas, before the Jain shrine of the next lines. Whether வலம்செயா (line 10) means they circled the temple or passed it without circling turns on the form; I read it as the poetic absolutive, having circled.
silappathikaram:10:1-14.event: Kovalan and Kannaki leave their Puhar mansion secretly before dawn and pass the Vishnu temple and the Buddhist viharas.

claims.claim: a deed of the past drives a person's departure on the path that leads to its fruit

silappathikaram:10:15-31.reading: They come to the Arhat shrine of those who gave up flesh and keep an unfailing vow, where lay votaries have set a shining stone seat for the Charanas who come at the festivals, worship it and circle it, and then flow out of the city's passages like a great river leaving the hills, past the outer wall of the king's pleasure garden where the southern breeze pays its tribute with spring.
silappathikaram:10:15-31.nuance: The seat is worshipped empty: it is set up against the chance (தகுதி) that the sky-walking Charanas will come, which prepares the Charana who appears on such a seat at line 161. உலக நோன்பிகள் are those who keep the vow while living in the world, the lay counterpart of the ascetics described in lines 15 to 17.
silappathikaram:10:15-31.event: The couple worship and circle the Charanas' stone seat at the Jain shrine and leave the city by the garden wall.
silappathikaram:10:15-31.unit_note: The boundary between the original units 15-29 and 30-51 is moved from after line 29 to after line 31: lines 28-31 are one clause ending at போகி (line 31), the departure past the garden wall.

silappathikaram:10:32-51.reading: Going west along the Kaveri's north bank they reach after one kaatham the flower grove of the Jain nun Kavunthi's retreat; Kannaki, aching in feet and waist, asks in her child's speech which of these is Madurai, and Kovalan laughs that it is thirty kaathams beyond their land; they worship the nun, who asks why people of their form, family, conduct and vow have left home like the afflicted, and Kovalan answers that he seeks wealth in old Madurai.
silappathikaram:10:32-51.nuance: Kannaki's question after one kaatham, and Kovalan's laughing answer that thirty is near, measure the distance between her sheltered life and the journey. Kavunthi credits the couple with a vow that never strays from the Great One's word (line 47), which counts them among the lay faithful. Kovalan's stated motive, wealth (வரைபொருள் வேட்கை), stands against the narrator's ஊழ்வினை at line 4.
silappathikaram:10:32-51.event: Kannaki asks how far Madurai is, the couple meet the Jain nun Kavunthi at her retreat, and Kovalan tells her he goes to Madurai for wealth.
silappathikaram:10:32-51.unit_note: Starts at line 32 because lines 30-31 were moved to the preceding unit; the unit still ends at line 51, where Kovalan's answer closes the exchange.

silappathikaram:10:52-67.reading: Kavunthi says the forest-broken country is hard going for the girl's small anklet feet and that they will not turn back though told to, so she too, wishing to hear dharma from the learned and praise the Knower, will go to Madurai with them; Kovalan worships her and says her grace would end his wife's distress, and she begins to list the dangers of the road if they take the delicate girl into the shady groves.
silappathikaram:10:52-67.nuance: The nun's motive for the journey is her own: to hear the teaching at Madurai (lines 56-59). Her joining makes her the couple's guardian on the road, the role she hands on in Madurai.
silappathikaram:10:52-67.event: Kavunthi decides to go with the couple to Madurai, and Kovalan accepts her as their guide.

silappathikaram:10:68-83.reading: Kavunthi warns that in the groves a pit dug for tubers and hidden under fallen champak pollen can trap the unwary, ripe jackfruit and thorny jack-seeds in the turmeric and ginger thickets can hurt, and if they take the fields instead a vaalai fish leaping from an otter's jaws may frighten the girl, and honey dripping from the cane may cloud the pond.

silappathikaram:10:84-97.reading: She goes on: the girl, thirsty past bearing, might scoop that honeyed water in her palm or step unknowing on lilies thick with bees, and on the shore a careless step may harm the crab and the snail, a grief that cannot be borne; since there is no path but fields and groves, Kovalan must read the signs with his beloved and avoid each one.
silappathikaram:10:84-97.nuance: The danger in lines 90-93 runs both ways: the step may hurt the girl and it may hurt the crab and the snail she does not see, and the nun counts the second as a sorrow beyond bearing. ஊழ் here (line 92) is the order of the steps, not fate. The warning against drinking honeyed water may reflect a Jain avoidance of honey, but the lines give thirst and confusion of mind (அறிவு அஞர்) as the danger, not a rule.

claims.claim: a careless step that harms even small creatures like the crab and the snail is a grief to be guarded against

silappathikaram:10:84-97.unit_note: The original unit 84-98 ends one line early, at line 97 (குறுகாது ஓம்புஎன), where Kavunthi's warning ends; line 98 begins the list of what she takes up for the road.

silappathikaram:10:98-114.reading: Kavunthi takes up her flawless begging bowl, the cloth for her shoulder and the peacock-feather brush, and praying that the god who is the meaning of the word be their companion they set out into the Chola country, where even when Saturn smokes, a comet shows and Venus moves south, the new flood of the Kaveri comes down with the hills' goods to meet the sea's wealth, so that only its roar is heard at the sluices and no water-lift creaks, among paddy, cane, lotus pools and waterbirds.
silappathikaram:10:98-114.nuance: The omens of lines 102-103 are the Sangam formula for drought, kept here to praise the Kaveri, which fails no one when the sky fails. மொழிப்பொருள் தெய்வம் (line 100) I take as the god whose word is the truth, but the phrase is compressed.
silappathikaram:10:98-114.event: Kavunthi takes her bowl, cloth and peacock-feather brush, and the three set out through the Kaveri's fields.
silappathikaram:10:98-114.unit_note: Starts at line 98 instead of 99: line 98 (தோம்அறு கடிஞையும் சுவல்மேல் அறுவையும்) is the first of the things Kavunthi takes up at line 99, so it is moved out of the preceding unit.

silappathikaram:10:115-131.reading: The fields ring with the many cries of geese, herons, waterhens and crows like the camp of a victorious king, with the shouting of the dark-handed labourers when a mud-caked buffalo rubbing against the granary spills its paddy, and with the new song of the field-women who, having drunk hot toddy, transplant seedlings with mud on their bangled arms.

silappathikaram:10:132-155.reading: With the plough festival of the ploughmen who wear arugu and lily, the reaping songs at the threshing floors and the drums of the kinai bards in their ears, the travellers go on without grief past the Brahmins' auspicious settlements, whose sacrificial smoke wraps the mansions like mist on hills under the tiger-flag king's might, and past the old towns of the Kaveri's sons, moving only a kaatham a day and halting many days.
silappathikaram:10:132-155.nuance: The Vedic sacrifice is praised as part of the land's good order (மங்கல மறையோர் இருக்கை) in the same journey that the Jain nun leads; the text sets the faiths side by side and does not weigh them here.
silappathikaram:10:132-155.event: The three travel slowly through the Chola country, a kaatham a day, halting many days.

silappathikaram:10:156-169.reading: One day, at a grove on a river island near a place where the gods dwell, a Charana appears on the stone seat set by the great ascetics, proclaiming the true dharma of the Great One's wonder; the travellers fall at his feet with Kavunthi praying that their old deed may perish, and though he knows by the lamp of his mind why they have come, he does not grieve, being a hero who has put away desire and hatred.
silappathikaram:10:156-169.nuance: The Charana foresees what is coming to the couple and says nothing of it; the narrator explains his silence by his freedom from desire and hatred (ஆர்வமும் செற்றமும்), not by indifference. Their prayer, பண்டைத் தொல்வினை பாறுக, asks for the very thing his sermon will say cannot be had.
silappathikaram:10:156-169.event: A Jain Charana appears on the stone seat, and the travellers and Kavunthi fall at his feet praying that their old deeds perish.

claims.claim: one who has put away desire and hatred does not grieve even when he foresees another's suffering

silappathikaram:10:156-169.unit_note: The original unit 156-170 ends one line early, at line 169 (விழுமம் கொள்ளான்): line 170 opens the Charana's speech to Kavunthi and is moved to the next unit.

silappathikaram:10:170-191.reading: The Charana tells Kavunthi that the strong deed, which will not go when bidden, comes back like a sown seed to face its doer and cannot be put off once it clings, that lives do not stay long in bodies, like a lamp set in a windy open place, and that, unless the light of the Veda spoken by the Lord reaches them, souls will not open the bundle of births; he names that Lord by a long run of titles, Knower, Jina, Siddha, Arhat, the one of eight qualities, Sankara, Isa, the self-born and four-faced.
silappathikaram:10:170-191.nuance: The verb ஊட்டும் is the patikam's (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும், line 57 of the patikam), so the epic's third moral is here given to a Jain sage as doctrine, with one addition the patikam lacks: a way out of birth through the Jina's word. The titles take names other schools use for their own gods (சங்கரன், ஈசன், சதுமுகன், வேத முதல்வன்) and claim them for the Arhat. The syntax of lines 174-175 is compressed; I read the lamp in the wind as the image of life in the body.

claims.claim: a strong deed, once sown like a seed, returns to its doer and cannot be put off when it clings
life stays in the body no longer than a lamp in a windy open place
souls are freed from the bundle of births only when the light of the Jina's spoken teaching reaches them

silappathikaram:10:170-191.unit_note: Runs from line 170 (moved from the preceding unit) to line 191, where the Charana's speech ends (பொதிஅறை யோர்என); lines 192-195 were moved to the next unit because they begin Kavunthi's reply.

silappathikaram:10:192-213.reading: Hearing the Charana, Kavunthi lays her hands on her head and vows that her ears open only to the word of the one who quenched the three, her tongue speaks only the thousand and eight names of the conqueror of desire, her eyes see only the feet of the conqueror of the five, her body touches earth only before his holy form, her hands join only for the Arhat, her head bears only his flower feet and her mind moves only for his word; the sage rises a cubit from the ground, blesses her that the bond which brings birth may perish, and goes through the sky, and the travellers worship and go on.
silappathikaram:10:192-213.nuance: The vow goes organ by organ, ears, tongue, eyes, body, hands, head, mind, and each line has the same 'only for him' (அல்லது) shape, so devotion is described as the closing of every sense to all else. The Charana's blessing names பாசம் and பவம்: the bond is what brings birth.
silappathikaram:10:192-213.event: Kavunthi vows every sense to the Arhat, and the Charana blesses her and departs through the sky.

claims.claim: the bond that brings rebirth can be destroyed

silappathikaram:10:192-213.unit_note: Starts at line 192 (சாரணர் வாய்மொழி கேட்டு), where Kavunthi's reply begins after the Charana's speech closes at line 191; ends as before at line 213.

silappathikaram:10:214-228.reading: Crossing the Kaveri by a ghat to its south bank, the three rest in a grove, where a wanton courtesan and an idle-tongued man come up, ask the fasting nun who these two, like Kama and his consort, are; when she answers that they are her children, human beings, and bids them stand off from the weary pair, the two jeer whether people born of one womb live together as man and wife, and call her learned.
silappathikaram:10:214-228.nuance: Kavunthi's 'my children' is the nun's shield for a married couple, and the mockers turn it into an insinuation of incest. நோற்றுஉணல் யாக்கை (line 223), the body that eats only after fasting, is how they address her, and her austerity is what gives force to what follows.
silappathikaram:10:214-228.event: A courtesan and a loose-tongued man mock Kavunthi and the couple, insinuating that the pair are siblings living as lovers.

silappathikaram:10:229-248.reading: Kannaki stops her ears and trembles before her husband; Kavunthi, calling the two scorners of her flower-garlanded girl, curses them to become old jackals of the thorn forest, and the curse that her penance gives takes hold; when the couple, trembling at the jackals' howls, plead that the improper words of those who have left the path are ignorance and ask her to name a time of release, she rules that, having fallen into low birth by ignorance, they shall suffer twelve months by the Uraiyur hedge and then regain their former form, and the three enter Uraiyur.
silappathikaram:10:229-248.nuance: Lines 233-234 use the same formula as the patikam's curse of the former birth (இட்ட சாபம் கட்டியது ஆகலின், patikam line 49), but this curse is given a term and a return to former form, at the plea of the very couple who were wronged. The pardon comes from the victims: it is Kovalan and Kannaki who name the insult ignorance, and Kavunthi takes their word (அறியாமையின், line 241) into her release.
silappathikaram:10:229-248.event: Kavunthi curses the two mockers into jackals and, at the couple's plea, sets a twelve-month term of release, and the three enter Uraiyur.

claims.claim: an ascetic's penance gives her curse the power to take hold
the wrong words of those who have left the right path should be taken as ignorance and pardoned

links.note: The ஊழ்வினை that drives the couple out of Puhar before dawn is the deed whose ripening time (வினைவிளை காலம்) the patikam gives as the reason the Pandya failed to inquire.
links.teaches: The epic names the past deed both at the first step out of the house and at the hour of the killing, so the whole journey is framed as one deed's ripening, while the travellers themselves give wealth as their reason.

links.note: The couplet says fate outruns any other plan; the narrator puts ஊழ்வினை behind a journey Kovalan plans, by his own word at line 51, to win back wealth.
links.teaches: The epic shows the couplet's claim working from inside a person's own scheme: the plan to recover wealth is not overtaken by fate but is the road fate travels.

gains.a: its passing word ஊழ்வினைக் கடைஇ gains the force of a stated rule that no counter-plan can outrun the deed
gains.b: the couplet's abstract 'it gets there first' gains a case where the victim's own design is the vehicle

links.note: The couplet says all living beings join hands to the one who does not kill and refuses flesh; the epic shows lay votaries worshipping the stone seat set for the flesh-renouncing Charanas even when none is there.
links.teaches: The couplet's hyperbole of universal worship becomes an institution in the epic: a built seat honoured in the ascetics' absence, which then becomes the place where a Charana actually appears at line 161.

gains.a: the empty seat gains its reason: the refusal of flesh is what earns such worship
gains.b: the couplet's worship gains a concrete form, a lay cult of the renouncers' seat

links.note: The couplet defines the good path (நல்லாறு, நெறி) as the way that keeps not killing anything in view; Kavunthi's road counsel makes that literal, warning that a careless step on the shore may harm the crab and the snail.
links.teaches: Read together, the couplet's path metaphor turns into an actual walk where every footfall must be watched, and the nun counts harm to a snail as a grief equal to the dangers to the traveller herself.

gains.a: the nun's warning gains its principle: the attention she asks for is the couplet's சூழும், a constant watch
gains.b: the couplet's யாதொன்றும் gains a case showing it reaches even crabs and snails underfoot

links.note: Both open on Venus straying south as the sign of drought and say the Kaveri still brings its flood.
links.teaches: The epic borrows the Pattinappalai's drought omen for the Kaveri on the road out of Puhar, so the couple's departure from the city is set in the same praise that once opened a poem about the city's wealth.

gains.a: the epic's omen list gains its source and sense as a Chola praise-formula for the river
gains.b: the Sangam formula gains a later use in a travel scene, where it marks the plenty the travellers are leaving behind

links.note: Both list Saturn smoking, a comet showing and Venus running south; Kapilar credits the rain that never failed in Pari's land to the king's straight sceptre, while the epic credits the Kaveri's flood to the river.
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows the same omen formula assigning the land's safety to different powers: to a just king in Purananuru 117, and to the river itself in the epic.

gains.a: the epic's omens gain their weight as signs that normally ruin a land unless something stronger holds
gains.b: Kapilar's poem gains a counter-case where the formula is used without any king's virtue as the cause

links.note: The patikam's third moral, ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும், reappears with the same verb ஊட்டும் in the Charana's sermon on the strong deed that will not go.
links.teaches: The poet's announced moral is put into the mouth of a Jain sage within the story, who adds what the patikam does not: that the Jina's word can end the births the deed feeds.

links.note: The quatrain says not even ascetics (உறுவர்) can remove what must befall; the epic shows an ascetic who sees the couple's coming fate by his inner lamp and tells them the deed cannot be put off.
links.teaches: The pair shows the quatrain's limit on ascetic power from the ascetic's side: the Charana knows, does not grieve, and states the rule himself instead of trying to avert the fate.

gains.a: the Charana's silence about the couple's fate gains a reason: by the quatrain's rule his knowing could not change it
gains.b: the quatrain's general uruvar gains a named scene where a seer meets those whose fate he foresees

links.note: The Charana says the strong deed cannot be put off once it clings and that release from births comes through the Jina's spoken teaching; Tirumular says that by Siva's grace deeds do not cling at all.
links.teaches: The two give incompatible accounts of whether a ripening deed can be stopped: for the Charana only the cycle of births can be ended, by teaching, while the deed must still be eaten; for Tirumular grace prevents the deed from clinging.

gains.a: the Charana's sermon gains a clear rival: what it denies is precisely the grace that removes karma
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a contemporary opponent for whom no god's grace stops a deed once sown

links.note: The couplet calls a head that does not bow to the eight-qualitied one as useless as a sense organ without sense; Kavunthi vows each organ, ears, tongue, eyes, body, hands, head and mind, to the Arhat alone.
links.teaches: The couplet's single comparison between the bowing head and a dead sense is worked out by the nun into a vow for every sense in turn, and the eight-qualitied one is named in the preceding sermon as the Jain Lord (எண்குணன், line 188).

gains.a: the nun's vow gains its root: a sense not turned to the Lord is as if it did not work
gains.b: the couplet's எண்குணத்தான் gains a reading in which a Jain voice claims the title for the Arhat

links.note: Both curses are told in the same formula, a curse given (இட்ட சாபம்) that took hold (கட்டியது); the former-birth curse on Kovalan has no term and ends in his never again being seen in human form, Kavunthi's has a term of twelve months and a return to former shape.
links.teaches: Just before Madurai the epic shows a curse that the wronged can soften and that ends in a restored body, so the reader meets the bounded curse first and the unbounded one, which no plea can term, at the story's end.

links.note: The couplet ranks those who fast below those who bear the harsh words of others; Kavunthi, whom the mockers address by her fasting body, curses them, and it is the insulted couple who ask that the words be taken as ignorance.
links.teaches: The epic splits the couplet's two figures between two people: the faster answers insult with a curse, and the forbearance the couplet ranks higher comes from the young couple who were insulted.

gains.a: the couple's plea gains a ranking: by the couplet their forbearance stands above the nun's austerity
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene showing that fasting and forbearance can come apart, with the insult aimed at the ascetic's wards and not at herself

links.note: The couplet says that crushing foes and raising those one loves come by tapas if one so intends; Kavunthi's penance gives her curse its hold and her word of release its power.
links.teaches: The epic shows both halves of the couplet in one act of one ascetic: the same tapas that turns the mockers into jackals sets the day they become human again.

gains.a: the phrase தவம்தரு சாபம் gains its doctrine: the curse is a use of the power tapas confers
gains.b: the couplet's 'if one intends' (எண்ணின்) gains a case where the ascetic does intend, and is then moved to limit what she intended

new_concepts.gloss: a curse, a word spoken in grief or anger that binds its object and comes to fruit, even in a later birth
the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (line 47; நோன்பிகள் at line 24)

source_issues: The edition prints 245 as the last line number, but the kaathai has 248 lines as cut; line numbers here are the core file's.
Lines 41, 51, 200 and 224 carry repaired encoding (a TSCII leftover and stray spaces), flagged by show; the repaired readings are used.
